title: Adaptive and Sustainability for Visual and Perceptive Comfort: Neuroscience and Architecture
central_proposition: An integrated methodological approach, informed by neuroscience and information theory, is proposed for lighting design to achieve visual and perceptive comfort, well-being, and energy sustainability through adaptivity, resilience, and dynamic brain plasticity, particularly in historical buildings.

concept_definitions.name: Light (physical quantity)
concept_definitions.definition: a small portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, between 380 nm and 800 nm, that can evoke a neural response from photoreceptors in the human retina and brain

concept_definitions.name: Lighting (design and application)
concept_definitions.definition: the design and application of electromagnetic radiation by means of the visual and thermal effects control for architectural and social benefits

concept_definitions.name: Neuroscience
concept_definitions.definition: the quest for understanding physiological and behavioral responses to the electromagnetic radiation and/or different indoor/outdoor luminous climate

concept_definitions.name: Neuroesthetics
concept_definitions.definition: cognitive neurosciences applications and to the well-known embodied cognition

concept_definitions.name: Embodied cognition
concept_definitions.definition: the feedback signals from the regions that involve the visual cortical areas and the cerebral sensomotory and premotory circuits in the presence of visual affordance of displayed stimulus

concept_definitions.name: Color (perceived)
concept_definitions.definition: has not a physical dimension: this means that it does not belong to the external world but to a psychophysical dimension, “created” by the brain

concept_definitions.name: Connectome
concept_definitions.definition: the informational neuro-electric current (electrical-wiring) that determines the dynamic traces of memories, transforming the mental structures into molecular structures

concept_definitions.name: Information theory (applied to lighting)
concept_definitions.definition: based on messages' transmission (set of signals) from a source (light), through a communication channel (object and/or artwork, visual exploration path) to a receiver (subject/observer)

concept_definitions.name: Common sense (communication experience)
concept_definitions.definition: the information transmitted that can be measured and assessed by means of the knowledge of all the visual and perceptive data concerning visual path and visual performance changes

concept_definitions.name: Modeling Index (M=Esc/Ev)
concept_definitions.definition: describes the balance between diffuse and directed light, i.e., the ratio of semi-cylindrical illuminance to vertical illuminance at a defined point

argument_structure: The paper establishes the interdisciplinary nature of light, lighting, and neuroscience, then details a methodological approach integrating experimental measurements (photometric, eye-tracking) and numerical simulations for lighting design. It presents case studies to demonstrate the application of this approach, focusing on adaptivity, sustainability, visual/perceptive comfort, and well-being. The argument posits that light is an information channel influencing cognitive processes, emotions, and behavior, and that lighting design should leverage this understanding for optimal human-centric outcomes and energy efficiency.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Light, as a physical stimulus, triggers neural responses in the retina and brain, leading to visual perception, cognitive processing, and affective states, influenced by both top-down (knowledge, prior experience) and bottom-up (light properties) processes. By understanding these neurophysiological mechanisms, lighting design can be optimized to regulate circadian rhythms, enhance cognitive performance, influence perception, evoke emotions (e.g., beauty mapped in the hippocampus), facilitate information transmission, promote sustainability through adaptive control, and support social interaction.

findings.antecedent: Optimal combination between natural and artificial light, occurring at the right time of day
findings.consequent: Regulation of circadian clock, mood, alertness, and activity level
findings.mechanism: Light, as a physical quantity, evokes neural responses from photoreceptors in the human retina and brain, influencing physiological and behavioral responses to luminous climate.
findings.quote: Health benefits, learning and cognitive improvement due to quality of light and lighting, and optimal combination between natural and artificial light, occurring at the right time of day, can help to regulate our circadian clock, mood, alertness, and activity level.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Many literature researches have demonstrated that technologies belonging to cognitive neuroscience can be used for lighting design [4-7].

findings.antecedent: Quality of light and lighting
findings.consequent: Learning and cognitive improvement
findings.mechanism: Light evokes neural responses in the retina and brain, influencing physiological and behavioral responses.
findings.quote: Health benefits, learning and cognitive improvement due to quality of light and lighting...
findings.empirical_support_cited: Many literature researches have demonstrated that technologies belonging to cognitive neuroscience can be used for lighting design [4-7].

findings.antecedent: Greater informative content of visual stimuli (e.g., architectural areas, objects, artworks, people movements)
findings.consequent: Visual explorations, number of fixations, vision and perception quality, mental elaboration, interpretation, and representation of cognitive processes
findings.mechanism: Information theory applied to lighting design, where light acts as a source transmitting signals through a communication channel (object/artwork, visual exploration path) to a receiver (subject/observer).
findings.quote: Research findings showed that all the visual explorations... happen because of their greatest informative content.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Research findings showed that all the visual explorations, the greater number of fixations, vision and perception quality, mental elaboration, interpretation and representation of cognitive processes, and perception of different building architectural areas, objects and/or artworks, and people movements and paths inside different environments happen because of their greatest informative content [12, 13].

findings.antecedent: Sensation of beauty (triggered by light)
findings.consequent: Activation of brain and visual-perceptive, cognitive-interpretative functions; well-being; prospective optimism; resilience differential
findings.mechanism: Beauty is physiologically mapped in the hippocampus, and its sensation/awareness, when triggered by light, activates specific brain networks (connectomic maps) that promote positive psychological states.
findings.quote: The sensation and awareness (consciousness) of beauty that light can trigger as an activator of brain and visual-perceptive, cognitive-interpretative functions, allow to outline important and new connectomic maps that are able of activating the well-being and development of a prospective optimism that intensifies and strengthens the resilience differential.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The method applications show how the concepts of sustainability and adaptivity derive from the sensation of beauty, physiologically mapped in the hippocampus.

findings.antecedent: Light (natural and/or artificial)
findings.consequent: Creation or recovery of atmospheres, suggestions, bright, pleasant, and comfortable environments
findings.mechanism: Light influences visual perception and aesthetic judgment, which are complex systems of top-down and bottom-up cognitive processes.
findings.quote: Tackling a lighting project is always a complex operation, because with light (natural and/or artificial) it is possible not only to respond to functional needs... but also to create or recover atmospheres and suggestions, as well as bright, pleasant, and comfortable environments.

findings.antecedent: Different illumination of the signifier (object/artwork)
findings.consequent: Alteration of meaning, interpretation, and perception by the observer
findings.mechanism: Light acts as an information channel, and changes in its properties (e.g., illuminant, color) affect the signals transmitted, influencing the mental representation of the perceptual-cognitive experience.
findings.quote: the application of our method can be useful to understand how much, where, and when a different illumination of the signifier (object/artwork) can alter the meaning and therefore the interpretation and perception of the one who uses it and observes it.
findings.empirical_support_cited: By means of practical experiences and tests, it was possible to evaluate the quality of light in different environments, which people surely appreciated because it is a part of that common sense of the communication experience.

findings.antecedent: Color of light radiation or an object
findings.consequent: Perceived color
findings.mechanism: Defined by the relative activity of three types of cones sensitive to different wavelengths; 'created' by the brain, not a physical dimension. Neural mechanisms transmit visual and color information to the occipital lobe (V1) and temporal lobe (V4) for complex analysis, enabling color constancy.
findings.quote: The color of a light radiation or an object is defined by the relative activity of three types of cones... But since this comparison is the true equivalent of the perceived color, color has not a physical dimension: this means that it does not belong to the external world but to a psychophysical dimension, “created” by the brain.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The neurosciences and deep sciences applied to vision show how the two types of photoreceptors, rods, and cones, respectively, used for vision at low luminance levels (night vision) and “blind" to color and the seconds for vision at high luminance levels (daylight) are the first neural structures involved in the color perception.

findings.antecedent: Light (as a physical element)
findings.consequent: Viewing and receiving information associated with a scene or illuminated objects; knowledge acquisition
findings.mechanism: Light excites millions of light-sensitive receptors in the retina, initiating an interpretation and transformation process of the external world that culminates in the cerebral cortex and behavioral responses.
findings.quote: Light should be understood as a physical element that makes it possible to view and receive the information associated with the scene or the illuminated objects, representing an essential vehicle of information and knowledge.

findings.antecedent: Visual signals (analogic)
findings.consequent: Neural signals (digital)
findings.mechanism: Transduction process involving encoding, transmission along nerve pathways, and parallel processing in visual stations, with selection of important information and rejection of redundant information.
findings.quote: The process of transduction of analogic signals into digital ones includes the encoding of the visual signals into neural signals, their transmission along the nerve pathways, and their parallel processing in the different visual stations, with the selection of that part of the information that is considered most important and attenuation or rejection of the others considered redundant.

findings.antecedent: Visual stimulation (e.g., light)
findings.consequent: Activation of occipital lobes; visual perception
findings.mechanism: Cortical afferents from the retina project to the occipital lobes, which serve as the first substrate for visual perception. This is part of the brain's connectome activation.
findings.quote: an activation of the occipital lobes is typical for those tasks in which there is a visual stimulation, which receives cortical afferents from the retina, so that it is the first substrate for visual perception.
findings.empirical_support_cited: This dynamic constitutes what the functional neuroimaging, the basic tool of cognitive neuroscience, calls the activation process of a network of brain areas (i.e., feedback, synchrony, and plasticity of the brain).

findings.antecedent: Interaction between logical cognitive processes and hot/cold ones (emotional, affective, interpretative functions)
findings.consequent: Mind operation of cleaning, pruning, and construction of information flows (inside to outside, outside to inside, inside to inside); modification of connectome
findings.mechanism: These processes are triggered by activators like light and synchronously modify the connectome, which is the informational neuro-electric current determining dynamic traces of memories.
findings.quote: There is always interaction between logical cognitive processes with hot/cold ones (emotional, affective, interpretative functions) which lead, by means of the mind operation of cleaning, pruning, and construction to the three understanding directions of the information flows... These processes are triggered by activators, such as light, and synchronously modify the connectome.

findings.antecedent: Light (as an information channel carrying signals with informational and cultural content)
findings.consequent: Sustainable lighting design (ability to carry information); reorganization of spaces and environments; creation of new pathways; new perceptions
findings.mechanism: Lighting design based on dynamic light control can leverage light's role as an information channel to influence how spaces are perceived and used, leading to adaptive and sustainable solutions.
findings.quote: If interaction between observer and object is a complex system of top-down and bottom-up cognitive processes, then sustainable lighting design should be conceived in its ability to carry information: i.e., light is an information channel that carries signals with informational and cultural content.

findings.antecedent: Plastic and resilient lighting design
findings.consequent: Tracing of enormous transformations in neural networks; cognitive retinal images; rediscovery of peculiarity of spaces and places
findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting design, by influencing neural networks, can 'write' new cognitive retinal images and guide the perception of spaces, adapting to changing experiences.
findings.quote: Nowadays, lighting design can “write" by tracing on the retina, in the memory networks, the enormous transformations we are experiencing, causing them to become cognitive retinal images and guiding us to the rediscovery of the peculiarity of spaces and places.

findings.antecedent: Effective lighting control and regulation systems; filtering and transforming natural light (e.g., plants, nanostructured materials, textiles) through digital technologies
findings.consequent: Visual and perceptive setting for reading, writing, museum itineraries, shopping, working; new proximity (visual and perceptive physical distance); creative emotional experience
findings.mechanism: These systems create dynamic and adaptive luminous environments that influence visual tasks, spatial perception, and emotional responses, leading to new forms of interaction with space.
findings.quote: Effective lighting control and regulation systems, filtering and transforming natural light... through digital technologies application, provide a visual and perceptive setting where reading and writing, museum itineraries, shopping, working, and any visual task becomes a new proximity as a new visual and perceptive physical distance and therefore a new creative emotional experience.

findings.antecedent: VLC (Visible Light Communication) integration on LED systems (compared to linear fluorescent systems)
findings.consequent: More uniform distribution of illuminance values; lower UGR (Unified Glare Rating) on worktops and floors; quality of vision on workstations; visual comfort; high contrast index; ergonomics of vision for long times
findings.mechanism: VLC-LED systems provide structured light that optimizes visual conditions.
findings.quote: The comparison between two solutions, the first with VLC integration on linear fluorescent systems and the second with VLC integration on LED systems, shows a more uniform distribution of illuminance values and lower UGR on the worktops and floors for the second solution (Fig. 28).
findings.empirical_support_cited: The comparison between two solutions... shows a more uniform distribution of illuminance values and lower UGR on the worktops and floors for the second solution (Fig. 28).

findings.antecedent: VLC-LED solution (compared to VLC-fluorescent)
findings.consequent: LENI (Lighting Energy Numeric Indicator)
findings.mechanism: Different energy consumption profiles for different lighting technologies.
findings.quote: for the VLC-LED solution is 20,04 kWh/m² year. This value is higher but absolutely comparable with that one calculated for VLC-fluorescent which is 19,04 kWh/m² year.
findings.empirical_support_cited: for the VLC-LED solution is 20,04 kWh/m² year. This value is higher but absolutely comparable with that one calculated for VLC-fluorescent which is 19,04 kWh/m² year.

findings.antecedent: Introduction of three-layer groups of tropical plants in window area (Scervino space)
findings.consequent: Reduction of illuminance levels near doors and windows (compared to surrounding zones); reduction of direct illuminance on south wall (33.83%); reduction of direct illuminance on west wall (35.43%)
findings.mechanism: Plants act as filters and transformers of natural light, controlling solar radiation and UV penetration.
findings.quote: the direct illuminance value on the south wall... is reduced by 33,83%; the corresponding value on the west wall... is reduced by 35,43% (Figs.25 and 26).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Although the illuminance levels near doors and windows are appreciably higher than in the surrounding zones, the corresponding values show a reduction of more than 50% compared to the existing state, due to the introduction of the three layer-groups of tropical plants.

findings.antecedent: Use of tropical plants for solar radiation control
findings.consequent: LENI value (Scervino space)
findings.mechanism: Plants reduce solar radiation, thus reducing the need for artificial lighting and associated energy consumption.
findings.quote: the LENI value obtained for the lighting solution was 42,92 kW/m² year, compared to 89,11 kW/m² year of the existing state; this fact shows an important energy consumption reduction of 51,84%.
findings.empirical_support_cited: the LENI value obtained for the lighting solution was 42,92 kW/m² year, compared to 89,11 kW/m² year of the existing state; this fact shows an important energy consumption reduction of 51,84%.

findings.antecedent: New lighting design (Florentine Historical Monastery Library) with sail systems and LED sources (functional-library scenario)
findings.consequent: LENI (Lighting Energy Numeric Indicator)
findings.mechanism: Optimal mix of natural and artificial light with efficient control and dimming systems, and innovative LED technologies.
findings.quote: LENI (kWh/year/m²) Existing State: 22-23; Functional Library: 10-15
findings.empirical_support_cited: Table 3 shows results comparison with the existing state: the appreciable, strong reduction of LENI, annual energy consumption, and costs can be noted.

findings.antecedent: New lighting design (Florentine Historical Monastery Library) with sail systems and LED sources (functional-library scenario)
findings.consequent: Energy consumption (kWh/year)
findings.mechanism: Optimal mix of natural and artificial light with efficient control and dimming systems, and innovative LED technologies.

findings.antecedent: New lighting design (Florentine Historical Monastery Library) with sail systems and LED sources (functional-library scenario)
findings.consequent: Costs (€/year)

findings.antecedent: New lighting design (Florentine Historical Monastery Library)
findings.consequent: Preventive protection for people and book heritage 'health and well-being'; visual quality; ergonomics
findings.mechanism: The design complies with standards for visual tasks, vision ergonomics, and well-being, and integrates preventive conservation.
findings.source: p. 18, "3.5 Combining Natural Light Control with Optic Fiber Textiles"
findings.quote: Results showed that the proposed lighting assures preventive protection for people and book heritage “health and well-being” but also visual quality and ergonomics.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Results showed that the proposed lighting assures preventive protection for people and book heritage “health and well-being” but also visual quality and ergonomics.

findings.antecedent: Modeling index (M=Esc/Ev) value within 0.8–1.3 (Florentine Historical Monastery Library)
findings.consequent: Optimal light mix; good distribution and uniformity; visual ergonomics; goodness of light modeling
findings.mechanism: The modeling index describes the balance between diffuse and directed light, which is crucial for visual comfort and perception.
findings.source: p. 18, "3.5 Combining Natural Light Control with Optic Fiber Textiles"
findings.quote: M index results compared with luminance and illuminance distribution, the local contrast index, and unified glare index prove light optimal mix, good distribution and uniformity, and visual ergonomics but also goodness of light modeling.
findings.empirical_support_cited: M index results compared with luminance and illuminance distribution, the local contrast index, and unified glare index prove light optimal mix, good distribution and uniformity, and visual ergonomics but also goodness of light modeling.

findings.antecedent: Modeling index values higher than 1.3
findings.consequent: Shadows appear very soft; 3D objects contour not clearly distinguishable from background
findings.mechanism: An imbalance in diffuse vs. direct light affects visual contrast and depth perception.
findings.quote: for modeling index values higher than 1,3, shadows appear very soft and the 3D objects contour are not clearly distinguishable from the background

findings.antecedent: Modeling index values lower than 0.8
findings.consequent: Perceived images with high contrast; harsh shadows
findings.mechanism: An imbalance in diffuse vs. direct light affects visual contrast and depth perception.
findings.quote: for values lower than 0,8, the perceived images are with a high contrast and shadows are very harsh.

findings.antecedent: Integration index value of a point in a spatial layout
findings.consequent: Accessibility and integration of that point in the system
findings.mechanism: The integration index quantifies how close a given point is from all other points, reflecting its topological depth and ease of access within the spatial layout.
findings.quote: The greater the integration index value of a point in a spatial layout is, the more accessible and integrated is in the system; vice versa the lower the value of the integration index is, the more isolated and segregated the point results.

findings.antecedent: Visual connections and visibility interactions (connectivity index) in museum spaces
findings.consequent: Human behavior
findings.mechanism: In museum contexts, the immediate visual field and intervisibility between points (connectivity) are more influential on visitor behavior than the overall accessibility of a point within the layout (integration).
findings.quote: This fact means that in museum spaces human behavior is more influenced by the visual connections and the visibility interactions... than by the shortest paths linking different points...
findings.empirical_support_cited: It was stronger than that one obtained for the integration index. This fact means that in museum spaces human behavior is more influenced by the visual connections and the visibility interactions (meaning the property, expressed by the connectivity index of a point to be visible to all the other points in space) than by the shortest paths linking different points (property expressed by the integration index; Fig. 23).

findings.antecedent: Colder light (e.g., VWh - Vivid White LED)
findings.consequent: Observer's perception; concentration; processing of visual stimuli; visual scanning pattern (numerous fixations oriented to specific AOI); information content transmission
findings.mechanism: Different light colors affect neural processing of visual information, influencing attention, cognitive engagement, and the perceived salience of visual stimuli.
findings.source: p. 24, "3.7 Light, Information, and Visual Perception"
findings.quote: With the vivid white LED, the best and consistent results were obtained: greater concentration, greater processing of visual stimuli, increased perception, and visual scanning pattern with numerous fixations oriented to a spe- cific AOI before moving to another.
findings.empirical_support_cited: With the vivid white LED, the best and consistent results were obtained: greater concentration, greater processing of visual stimuli, increased perception, and visual scanning pattern with numerous fixations oriented to a spe- cific AOI before moving to another.

findings.antecedent: Lighting design (Specola Museum)
findings.consequent: LENI value
findings.mechanism: Optimized lighting solutions reduce energy consumption.
findings.source: p. 21, "3.6 Science of Anatomy and Light"
findings.quote: The LENI value for the new design is 7,53 kWh/m² year, for the existing state 32,30 kWh/m² year.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The LENI value for the new design is 7,53 kWh/m² year, for the existing state 32,30 kWh/m² year.

findings.antecedent: Lighting design (Specola Museum)
findings.consequent: Visitor experience (perceptive, tactile, kinesthetic, emotional, historical-cultural evocative experience); interest; imagination; enjoyment
findings.mechanism: Light guides the visitor's attention and interaction, transforming the visit from a serial observation to an immersive, multi-sensory experience.
findings.source: p. 21, "3.6 Science of Anatomy and Light"
findings.quote: The visit to the museum is not identified as an observation of an almost serial succession of works but as a real perceptive, tactile, kinesthetic, emotional, and historical-cultural evocative experience guided by light capable of arousing interest, the imagination, and perhaps even the enjoyment of visitors (Fig. 15).
findings.empirical_support_cited: The visit to the museum is not identified as an observation of an almost serial succession of works but as a real perceptive, tactile, kinesthetic, emotional, and historical-cultural evocative experience guided by light capable of arousing interest, the imagination, and perhaps even the enjoyment of visitors (Fig. 15).

findings.antecedent: Quality light (that everyone likes)
findings.consequent: Fundamental guide for setting up, exhibition, and museography projects
findings.mechanism: Light influences perception and attention, making it a powerful tool to direct visitor experience and highlight significant aspects of an exhibition.
findings.quote: but when it is designed for well-lighting, it can be a fundamental guide for the project of setting up, exhibition, and museography, based on quality light that everyone likes...
findings.empirical_support_cited: The results assessment, combining visual mapping with eye tracker data (Fig. 24), highlighted that when light is not designed to see well (i.e., for well-lighting and well-being), the energy linked to the vision is dispersed on boundaries... but when it is designed for well-lighting, it can be a fundamental guide for the project of setting up, exhibition, and museography, based on quality light that everyone likes...

findings.antecedent: Light not designed for well-lighting and well-being
findings.consequent: Energy linked to vision dispersed on boundaries (areas of little significance)
findings.mechanism: Ineffective lighting fails to direct attention to intended areas, leading to dispersed visual processing and reduced cognitive efficiency.
findings.quote: when light is not designed to see well... the energy linked to the vision is dispersed on boundaries (e.g., areas of little significance of the artwork and/or the surrounding museum space)
findings.empirical_support_cited: The results assessment, combining visual mapping with eye tracker data (Fig. 24), highlighted that when light is not designed to see well (i.e., for well-lighting and well-being), the energy linked to the vision is dispersed on boundaries (e.g., areas of little significance of the artwork and/or the surrounding museum space)

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Dynamic lighting designs that integrate natural and artificial light, optimized for circadian regulation, will lead to improved mood, alertness, and activity levels in occupants.

Lighting designs that enhance the 'informative content' of architectural elements and artworks will result in increased visual exploration, more fixations, and higher quality of perception and mental elaboration.

Lighting interventions that trigger the 'sensation of beauty' (e.g., through specific light colors or distributions) will activate the hippocampus and associated brain networks, leading to measurable increases in well-being, prospective optimism, and resilience.
VLC-LED lighting systems will demonstrate superior performance in terms of illuminance uniformity, glare reduction, visual comfort, and contrast compared to VLC-fluorescent systems.

The strategic integration of tropical plants in architectural spaces will significantly reduce solar radiation and UV penetration, leading to a measurable decrease in lighting energy consumption (LENI) and improved thermal comfort.
Lighting designs that achieve a modeling index (M=Esc/Ev) between 0.8 and 1.3 will be associated with optimal light mix, good distribution, uniformity, and visual ergonomics.

In museum environments, visitor behavior (e.g., movement paths, attention allocation) will be more strongly influenced by visual connections and intervisibility (connectivity index) than by overall spatial accessibility (integration index).

Colder light temperatures (e.g., Vivid White LED) will lead to higher observer concentration, greater processing of visual stimuli, and more focused visual scanning patterns on areas of interest compared to warmer light temperatures.
bridge_warrants: The paper connects neuroscience (brain plasticity, connectome, photoreceptors, hippocampus) with architectural lighting design.
It links information theory to visual perception and communication in built environments.
It integrates concepts of sustainability (energy saving, adaptive reuse) with human-centric outcomes (comfort, well-being, cognitive performance).
It applies space syntax techniques to understand human visual behavior and movement in relation to lighting.
It uses embodied cognition to explain how feedback signals from visual cortical areas and sensomotor circuits influence perception.
It connects the sensation of beauty to physiological mapping in the hippocampus, linking aesthetics to neurobiology.
It uses constructal theory to explain the natural evolution of systems towards maximizing energy and matter flows, applying it to lighting design for information transmission.
methodological_critiques: The paper implies that traditional lighting design is insufficient by proposing a new 'integrated methodological approach' that goes beyond functional needs to include cognitive and emotional aspects, suggesting a critique of existing, less holistic methods.
model_structure: The proposed 'integrated methodological approach' for lighting design involves: 1) A Knowledge Base encompassing luminous climate, building history, and neurosciences of vision. 2) Experimental Measurements using photometric, colorimetric, radiometric tools, psychophysical tests, eye-tracking, and user behavior detection systems. 3) Numerical Simulation via 3D architectural modeling and global illumination models, calibrated with experimental data. 4) Design Principles emphasizing light as an information channel, dynamic LED lighting, space syntax for visual mapping, human-centric outcomes, integration of natural elements, and creation of immersive emotional experiences.
